text: For several days Giovanni avoided the window, yet the image of Beatrice, at once lovely and terrible, burned in his mind like a fever he could neither cure nor resist. <break time="0.8s" /> One day, meeting Baglioni in the street, he saw Rappaccini pass by and fix upon him a look so coldly searching that it seemed to examine him as a specimen rather than a man. <break time="0.8s" /> He is making you the subject of one of his experiments, whispered the professor, who resolved, for the sake of his old friends son, to thwart the scheme, whatever it might be. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon afterward old Lisabetta, the landlady, whispered that she knew a private door into the garden, and for a gold coin she led the trembling youth through it. <break time="0.8s" /> Inside, every plant seemed fierce and unnatural, as if it had been created by mixing different species, and Giovanni felt that the garden was less the work of nature than of science. <break time="0.8s" /> When he said he had heard of her deep learning in botany, Beatrice laughed and begged him to believe nothing of her save what he saw with his own eyes. <break time="0.8s" /> Must I then believe all that I have seen, he asked, and she answered that what met his senses might be false in essence, but that her words were true from the depths of her heart outward. <break time="0.8s" /> But when he reached toward the purple shrub, she shrieked, Touch it not, It is fatal, and seized his hand, and the next morning four small purple marks, like the prints of slender fingers, burned upon it.
